explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "Tychicus will tell you all the news about me." Paul is locked up far from Colossae, so Tychicus is the walking, talking news update. No scrolling, no refreshing, just a brother at your door with the full story.

Nice guess, friend, but nothing in these verses mentions elders. Paul says Tychicus "will tell you all the news about me." So the visit is about Paul and how he's doing. If you showed up to my bakery expecting a lecture and got a plate of dough instead, you'd be confused too.

I see where you were headed, baker, but there's no offering in these verses. Paul says Tychicus "will tell you all the news about me." The man is carrying news, not a collection plate. Picture him knocking and the Colossians asking, "Wait, where's the news?" Awkward.

Yes, baker! Paul says he sent Tychicus "that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts." So the trip carries news and a lift for the heart. Some visitors leave you tired, but this one is sent to leave people better than he found them.

Close in sound, friend, but that's not the word. Paul says Tychicus is sent "that he may encourage your hearts." Nobody is handing out a pop quiz here. The trip is meant to build the Colossians up, not grade them.

Good try, baker, but Tychicus isn't there to dig around. Paul says he is sent "that he may encourage your hearts." He's not searching anybody's heart like I search the couch for a lost timer. He's there to give them courage.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "You have already received instructions about him: If he comes to you, welcome him." The word was already out before Mark ever got there. That's a heads-up with a warm welcome built right in.

Not quite, friend. The instruction in the text is "If he comes to you, welcome him." Nothing here says to ship Mark off to Paul. The Colossians are told to open the door, not forward him like a package.

Nice thought, baker, but no letters get mentioned for Mark. Paul says, "If he comes to you, welcome him." That's the whole instruction. Welcome first, and I'd say mail can wait until after he sits down.

Not this time, baker. Paul says the opposite: "These are the only Jews among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me." A comfort, not a worry. If I ever got called a comfort, I'd frame it and hang it over my ovens.

Right, baker. Paul says of Aristarchus, Mark and Justus, "they have been a comfort to me." So the text says comfort, not worry. Being a comfort to a man in chains is a pretty good thing to have written about you.

explanations.answer: To stand mature in God's will
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Epaphras is wrestling in prayer "so that you may stand mature and fully assured in the full will of God." That's a prayer for growing up in the faith and standing firm. He's not praying for a shortcut, just for them to stand steady.

explanations.answer: To stay safe from all trouble
explanations.explanation: Good heart, friend, but that's not what the text says. Epaphras prays "so that you may stand mature and fully assured in the full will of God." Safety from every bump isn't in the verse. He's praying for them to stand strong.

Fair guess, baker, but numbers aren't mentioned. Epaphras wrestles in prayer "so that you may stand mature and fully assured in the full will of God." He's after their maturity, not a bigger crowd. Quality over quantity, like a good batch.

explanations.answer: Have it read in another church
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul says, "After this letter has been read among you, make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans." So this letter was meant to travel. Mail that gets passed along is pretty great.

explanations.answer: Keep it safe with the elders
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Paul says to make sure the letter "is also read in the church of the Laodiceans." Elders aren't mentioned in that verse. This letter isn't meant to sit on a shelf. It's meant to go out the door.

Good try, baker, but no return trip is mentioned. Paul says the letter should be "read in the church of the Laodiceans." So the next stop is Laodicea, not a trip back to his prison. This letter has places to be.
Careful there, baker. Paul says the opposite: "…that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea." He wants them to read it, not skip it. Skipping mail was never part of the plan.
Yes, baker! Paul tells them to "…read the letter from Laodicea." Skipping it isn't on the table. So letters go back and forth, and the Colossians get a letter to read too.

That's right, baker. The message is, "See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord." Paul wants Archippus to finish what he was given. I think that's the kind of nudge that sticks with a man.

Nice try, friend, but there's no handoff in the text. The message is, "See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord." It's Archippus's job to finish. Nobody's taking his spot.

explanations.answer: Rest from it for a while
explanations.explanation: Rest is good, baker, but that's not this message. Paul says, "See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord." The word is complete it, not set it down. Time to finish the batch.

That's right, baker. Paul writes, "This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. Remember my chains." He's writing from a prison, so those chains were real. I think it's a quiet, heavy line, and it deserves a quiet moment.
Not this time, baker. Paul writes, "This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. Remember my chains." So he does ask them to remember his chains. It's a short line, but it's right there in the text.
